cards.q: What is the embryological origin and physiological gland type of the female breast?
cards.a: It originates as a specialized **ectodermal derivative** functioning physiologically as a **modified sweat gland (exocrine gland)**.

cards.q: When does primitive mammary tissue first become detectable during embryonic development?
cards.a: By the **6th gestational week**.

cards.q: What are the milk lines (mammary ridges) and what is their normal developmental fate in humans?
cards.a: They are bilateral **ectodermal thickenings** running from the **axillae down to the groins**; only the **middle part of the upper 1/3** persists into the mature breast, while cranial and caudal segments undergo apoptosis.

cards.q: What congenital condition results from persistent ectodermal nests along the milk lines, and what is its common diagnostic pitfall?
cards.a: It leads to **polythelia (supernumerary nipples)**, which is frequently mistaken on physical exam for **melanocytic nevi (moles)**.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of newly acquired, unilateral nipple inversion in an adult woman?
cards.a: It is a major red flag for underlying **breast carcinoma**, caused by tumor infiltration and **desmoplastic cicatricial traction** of lactiferous ducts.

cards.q: What anatomical muscle anomaly strictly defines Poland syndrome?
cards.a: Congenital absence of the **sternocostal head of the pectoralis major**, while the **clavicular head** and the **latissimus dorsi** are completely spared.

cards.q: Which associated congenital musculoskeletal defects are seen in Poland syndrome?
cards.a: Ipsilateral **breast hypoplasia/amazia**, absence of **ribs 2 to 4**, chest wall depression, and upper extremity **syndactyly or brachydactyly**.

cards.q: What is polymazia and how does it respond physiologically to pregnancy?
cards.a: The presence of **accessory breasts**, which contain functional glandular tissue that **enlarges during pregnancy** and **undergoes lactation during the puerperium**.

cards.q: What is the anatomical relationship of the breast to the thoracic fasciae, and what is the key exception?
cards.a: The breast lies entirely within the **superficial fascia**, EXCEPT for the **axillary tail of Spence**, which pierces the deep axillary fascia through the **foramen of Langer**.

cards.q: What is the retromammary space and what is its clinical significance?
cards.a: A loose areolar tissue cleft between the deep surface of the breast and the **pectoral fascia**, allowing **free physiological mobility** of the gland over the chest wall.

cards.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of the resting female breast on the chest wall?
cards.a: Vertically from the **2nd rib to the 6th rib**, and horizontally from the **lateral sternal border** to the **midaxillary line** (does not reach the posterior axillary line).

cards.q: To which peripheral anatomical structures does microscopic breast parenchyma routinely outstretch beyond its gross boundaries?
cards.a: Superiorly to the **clavicle**, inferiorly to the **rectus sheath**, medially to the **midline**, and laterally to the anterior border of the **latissimus dorsi**.

cards.q: What is the functional and histopathological unit of the mammary gland?
cards.a: The **terminal ductal lobular unit (TDLU)**, which is the microscopic epicenter where lobules drain into terminal ductules and the origin of **> 90% of breast pathologies**.

cards.q: What structures prevent breast sagging, and what causes clinical ptosis?
cards.a: The **suspensory ligaments of Cooper**; degradation of their **collagen and elastin fibers** combined with parenchymal atrophy leads to **ptosis** (corrected surgically via **mastopexy**).

cards.q: What is the primary arterial supply to the breast and what percentage of blood flow does it provide?
cards.a: The **internal mammary artery (internal thoracic artery)**, which delivers **50% to 60%** of total mammary blood flow via anterior perforators (primarily intercostal spaces 2-4).

cards.q: Which arterial branch of the axillary artery supplies the lateral quadrants of the breast?
cards.a: The **lateral thoracic artery**, arising from the **2nd part of the axillary artery**.

cards.q: How does breast carcinoma metastasize to the axial skeleton without involving the lungs?
cards.a: Via posterior intercostal veins communicating directly with **Batson's vertebral venous plexus**, which contains **valveless (avalvular)** veins that allow direct retrograde tumor embolization to the spine, pelvis, and skull.

cards.q: What percentage of mammary lymphatic drainage flows to the axillary lymph nodes versus internal mammary nodes?
cards.a: Approximately **75%** drains to the **axillary lymph nodes**, while **20%** drains to the **internal mammary nodes** (primarily from the medial quadrants).

cards.q: What is the key anatomical landmark used to define Berg's surgical levels of axillary lymph nodes?
cards.a: The **pectoralis minor muscle** (never the pectoralis major).

cards.q: How are Berg's axillary lymph node levels classified relative to the pectoralis minor muscle?
cards.a: **Level I** is **lateral** to pectoralis minor; **Level II** is **behind/deep** to pectoralis minor (including Rotter's nodes); **Level III** is **medial** to pectoralis minor.

cards.q: Which lymph node groups are found within Berg's Level I axillary station?
cards.a: The **anterior (pectoral)**, **posterior (subscapular)**, and **lateral (brachial/axillary vein)** groups.

cards.q: What is the single most prevalent and crucial presenting symptom of breast pathology?
cards.a: A discrete **breast mass**, which demands prompt diagnostic exclusion of **malignancy**.

cards.q: What is the primary imaging modality of choice for evaluating a breast mass in a woman under 35 years old?
cards.a: **Breast Ultrasound (Sonomammography)**, preferred due to the high density of fibroglandular breast tissue in young females.

cards.q: What is the initial imaging modality of choice for investigating a breast mass in females aged ≥ 35–40 years?
cards.a: **Digital Mammography (low-dose X-ray)**, because radiodense fibroglandular parenchyma is gradually replaced by **radiolucent fat**.

cards.q: What are the typical clinical features of a hard fibroadenoma?
cards.a: Occurs in women aged **16–25 years**, palpates as **rubbery firm**, measures **< 5 cm**, is smooth, and is hypermobile (the classic **"breast mouse"**).

cards.q: How does cystosarcoma phyllodes (phyllodes tumor) clinically differ from a typical fibroadenoma?
cards.a: It arises in women aged **> 40 years**, presents as a **very large/massive**, bosselated mass with rapid growth, stretched skin, and dilated veins, and can behave as a sarcoma that metastasizes **hematogenously**.

cards.q: What is the most common causative organism of acute lactational mastitis and breast abscess?
cards.a: **Staphylococcus aureus**, which enters via **nipple abrasions or fissures** and releases coagulase and hyaluronidase enzymes.

cards.q: What is the primary management for milk engorgement versus acute breast abscess?
cards.a: Milk engorgement requires **continued breast emptying (feeding/pumping)** and warm compresses; an acute abscess requires **surgical drainage (I&D or US-guided aspiration)** plus systemic antibiotics.

cards.q: What is an antibioma (chronic pyogenic abscess) and why is it surgically significant?
cards.a: A sterile, thick-walled mass that develops when an acute abscess is treated with **systemic antibiotics without surgical drainage**, which notoriously **clinically mimics breast carcinoma**.

cards.q: What is duct ectasia (periductal/plasma cell mastitis) and its characteristic nipple finding?
cards.a: Dilation of major subareolar ducts filled with inspissated debris that ruptures to trigger plasma cell inflammation and fibrosis, typically producing a **transverse, slit-like nipple retraction**.

cards.q: What does ANDI stand for, and what is its underlying hormonal etiology?
cards.a: **Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution** (fibrocystic disease); caused by **excess or hypersensitivity to estrogen** unopposed by progesterone.

cards.q: What are the four histopathological components of fibrocystic disease (ANDI)?
cards.a: 1) **Adenosis**, 2) **Epitheliosis**, 3) **Fibrosis**, and 4) **Cyst formation** (producing classic "blue-domed cysts of Bloodgood").

cards.q: What is the classic clinical symptom triad of fibrocystic disease (ANDI)?
cards.a: 1) **Cyclical mastalgia**, 2) **Nipple discharge**, and 3) **Diffuse nodularity** (described as bilateral "lumpy, cobblestone" texture peaking premenstrually).

cards.q: What are the three components of the Triple Assessment Protocol for evaluating breast lesions?
cards.a: 1) **Clinical examination** (inspection & palpation), 2) **Radiological imaging** (US and/or mammogram), and 3) **Pathological biopsy** (core needle biopsy or FNAC).
